specAnchors.text: know that an addition polymer is formed by joining up many small molecules called monomers
understand how to draw the repeat unit of an addition polymer, including poly(ethene), poly(propene), poly(chloroethene) and (poly)tetrafluoroethene
understand how to deduce the structure of a monomer from the repeat unit of an addition polymer and vice versa

primer.text: You already know from Alkenes that the C=C double bond is reactive and can open up to add other atoms across it. Addition polymerisation is that same reactivity put to work on a grand scale, with each alkene opening to grip its neighbours. This note shows how the giant chains form, how to draw them, and how to read them backwards.

modules.title: Monomers
modules.opening: Polymers are the giant molecules behind plastics, polystyrene and nylon, and this lesson introduces their recipe. Every polymer is assembled from huge numbers of small starter molecules called monomers, linked end to end by covalent bonds. The reaction needs demanding conditions, and it comes in two natural varieties: manufactured and biological.
keyPoints: A polymer is a large molecule of high relative molecular mass, built from many joined monomers.
The process of joining monomers together is called addition polymerisation.
Each monomer becomes a repeat unit, connected to its neighbours by covalent bonds.
Polymerisation reactions usually need high pressures and a catalyst.
Synthetic polymers are manufactured, like plastics and nylon, while nature makes natural or biological polymers.

low.restatement: Many small monomer molecules join end to end into one long polymer chain of repeating units.
low.analogy: It is like clipping train carriages together: each carriage is a monomer, the couplings are covalent bonds, and the coupled line is the polymer.
low.examPointer: Expect to name everyday polymers, such as plastics and polystyrene, and to state what monomers are.

medium.restatement: Addition polymerisation links monomers through covalent bonds under high pressure with a catalyst, producing molecules of high relative molecular mass; the same chemistry occurs in nature as well as in factories.
medium.analogy: Think of a paper chain: each loop is a monomer, the staples are covalent bonds, and the finished garland is far longer than any single loop.
medium.examPointer: Keep the terms straight: the monomer is the starter molecule, and the repeat unit is its pattern inside the chain.

modules.title: Drawing polymers
modules.opening: The second lesson turns to drawing: how a stream of alkene monomers becomes a polymer chain on paper. The trick is the C=C double bond, which opens up to link each monomer to its neighbours. Naming follows a simple pattern too, with poly- fixed to the front of the monomer's name.
keyPoints: Addition polymerisation only works with monomers that contain a C=C double bond.
One of the two bonds in each C=C breaks, forming the bond to the adjacent monomer.
The resulting polymer chain contains single bonds only.
The polymer's name takes the monomer's name in brackets with poly- added in front.
Propene monomers form polypropene, and ethene monomers form polyethene, as the note's two examples.

low.restatement: The C=C double bond in each monomer opens, one of its two bonds links to the next monomer, and the chain that results has only single bonds.
low.analogy: Picture velcro strips: only strips with the hook side can join, and once joined the hooks are used up, leaving smooth fabric along the chain.
low.examPointer: Practise all four named polymers: poly(ethene), poly(propene), poly(chloroethene) and (poly)tetrafluoroethene.

medium.restatement: Only monomers carrying a C=C bond can add to the chain, because breaking one bond of the pair frees each end to bond to neighbours; groups attached to the alkene simply ride along, and naming brackets the monomer name behind poly-.
medium.analogy: Think of unzipping a jacket halfway: the opened teeth fasten onto the next jacket, and the embroidered patches hang wherever they started.
medium.examPointer: In diagrams, make sure one of the two C=C bonds is the one shown breaking, and that the polymer shows single bonds throughout.

modules.title: Deducing monomers and repeat units
modules.opening: The final skill runs in both directions: given a monomer, draw the repeat unit; given a repeat unit, recover the monomer. Three changes do all the work — swap the bond order, adjust the end bonds, and mind the subscript n. Get those right and every named polymer is within reach.
keyPoints: To draw a repeat unit, change the monomer's double bond to a single bond.
Add a bond to each end, and let them extend outside the brackets.
A subscript n on the bottom right shows that a large number of repeat units are present.
The other groups keep the same order they had around the double bond in the monomer.
To recover the monomer, change the single bond back to a double bond and remove the end bonds and the n.

low.restatement: Monomer to repeat unit: the double bond becomes single, add extension bonds past the brackets and the subscript n; repeat unit to monomer: reverse the steps.
low.analogy: It works like a two-way recipe: fold a page in half, tuck the ends under the clip, and unfold the same page again to recover it.
low.examPointer: The commonest mark loss is forgetting the extension bonds outside the brackets or the subscript n, so check both every time.

medium.restatement: The monomer's double bond and the repeat unit's single bond are the same linkage in two states: converting one to the other, adding or removing the end bonds and the subscript n, is the entire change, with every attached group kept in order.
medium.analogy: Picture a zip on a backpack: zipped is the repeat unit with its extension bonds, unzipped is the monomer with its double bond, and the same teeth change state without rearranging.
medium.examPointer: Deduce monomers from repeat units by reopening the double bond exactly between the two bracketed carbons, keeping attached groups in the same positions.

glossary.definition: A small molecule that joins with many others to build a polymer.
A large molecule of high relative molecular mass made from linked monomers.
The process of joining many monomers into a polymer; with C=C monomers it is called addition polymerisation.
The pattern of one monomer as it appears inside the polymer chain.
Made by people; synthetic polymers such as plastics are manufactured rather than found in nature.
The bonds drawn sticking out beyond the brackets of a repeat unit, showing the chain continues.
